questions.question: In 1856 the Austrian monk Gregor Mendel began research using pea plants that led to a model for inheritance. Which of the following techniques ensured the data he obtained was **reliable**?
questions.answer: **A.** Reliability comes from repetition and large sample sizes. The other options control variables (validity).
options: He bred hundreds of plants and tabulated each outcome.
He ensured all plants self-pollinated by covering them with plastic bags.
He ensured pure breeding lines by previously breeding each variety for 2 years.
He kept plants isolated in a greenhouse to prevent accidental cross-pollination.

questions.question: The image shows a method of reproduction. When is this method of reproduction most useful?
questions.answer: **A.** Runners are asexual reproduction: many genetically identical offspring quickly, which suits a stable environment the parent is already adapted to.
options: The environment is stable and numbers can be increased very quickly.
The environment is constantly changing and numbers need to be increased.
The environment is stable and new plants with significant variation can be produced.
The environment is changing moderately fast and numbers need to increase to keep up with this change.

questions.question: A segment of DNA is "switched on" to produce a polypeptide. The polypeptide is then made into the desired protein, which functions as an enzyme to control the production of other cellular molecules. Identify the process described.
questions.answer: **B.** Using a gene's information to make a functional product is gene expression.

questions.question: The diagram represents three processes that occur during reproduction. Which processes contribute to variation between individuals?
questions.answer: **B.** Process 1 (meiosis) produces varied gametes and process 2 (fertilisation) combines them randomly. Process 3 (mitosis) produces identical cells.

questions.question: A student drew the incomplete diagram of DNA shown. Which option correctly completes labels 1, 2, 3 and 4?
questions.answer: **A.** 1 is deoxyribose sugar; thymine pairs with adenine; guanine pairs with cytosine; the circled unit of phosphate, sugar and base is a nucleotide.

questions.question:
The table compares two marsupials.

| | Long-tailed planigale | Tammar wallaby |
|---|---|---|
| Distribution | Northern Australia | South-west Australia |
| Mass (g) | 4.0 | 4800 |
| Body heat produced (J g$^{-1}$ h$^{-1}$) | 29.9 | 5.8 |

Predict which animal will have the greater difficulty maintaining body temperature when the ambient temperature is 10 °C.
questions.answer:
**D.** A large surface area to mass ratio means heat is lost rapidly relative to the body's size.

*Note: the school's key gives B. The wallaby's lower heat production per gram goes with much lower heat loss; the planigale, with nine times the surface area per gram, has the greater difficulty.*
options: Tammar wallaby, because it has a larger body to keep warm.
Tammar wallaby, because it produces less body heat per gram.
Planigale, because it normally lives in tropical northern Australia.
Planigale, because it has a greater surface area per unit body mass.

questions.question: The graph shows the change in numbers of a fruit fly population that was sprayed with an insecticide in the first year of the investigation and again five years later. What is the reason for the **small** drop in numbers after the second spraying?
questions.answer: **D.** The first spraying selected for resistant flies, which survived and reproduced, so most of the later population is unaffected.
options: The flies become immune to the insecticide.
The insecticide was more concentrated at the first spraying.
There is a higher percentage of resistant flies in the population.

questions.question: Which graph best shows the relationship between external temperature and body temperature for an endotherm and an ectotherm?
questions.answer: **D.** The endotherm keeps a constant high body temperature while the ectotherm's body temperature follows the external temperature.

questions.question:
The table shows death rates per 100 000 people aged 45–64.

| Cause of death | Non-smoker male | Non-smoker female | Smoker male | Smoker female |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lung cancer | 10 | 5 | 90 | 20 |
| Other cancers | 150 | 200 | 180 | 180 |
| Cardiovascular disease | 450 | 140 | 800 | 250 |
| Total deaths | 610 | 345 | 1070 | 450 |

Which is a reasonable conclusion from these data?
questions.answer: **D.** Lung cancer deaths are much higher in smokers. Rates of this kind show an association (a risk factor) but do not by themselves prove cause.
options: Cigarette smoking is a risk factor for lung cancer.

questions.question: DNA profiling was used to test which of three men is the father of a child. Which individual is most likely to be the father?
questions.answer: **C.** Every band in the child that is not found in the mother appears in William's profile. A child's profile need not match either parent exactly.
options: None of them, as no man's profile exactly matches the child's

questions.question: Which of the following can introduce new alleles into a population's gene pool?
questions.answer: **A.** Mutation creates new alleles and gene flow brings in alleles from other populations. Drift and selection only change frequencies.

questions.question: Genetically identical plants have been produced for centuries by taking multiple cuttings from one plant. Which term describes this process?
questions.answer: **C.** Each cutting grows into a genetically identical whole organism.

questions.question: Many people may decide not to have children based on the results of genetic screening for particular genetic diseases. What impact will this have on human evolution?
questions.answer: **A.** Fewer copies of the allele are passed on, changing allele frequency. It is unlikely to be lost completely (carriers and new mutations remain).
options: It will alter the frequency of an allele and will therefore have an impact on future human evolution.
It will have no impact, since the genes or DNA are not altered by the testing.
It will increase genetic variation in the human population and so have an impact.
It will result in complete loss of an allele from the population and so have an impact.

questions.question: The genetic diversity index of four platypus populations is I: 0.419, II: 0.606, III: 0.032, IV: 0.431 (the lower the index, the less variation). Which population is at greatest risk of extinction due to genetic factors?
questions.answer: **C.** Population III has very little variation, so it is least able to adapt to change.

questions.question: Which term describes a molecule capable of triggering an immune response?
questions.answer: **A.** An antigen is a molecule recognised by the immune system that triggers a response.

questions.question: Students compared the number of bacteria in bottled and tap water. They spread 1 mL of tap water on one agar plate and 1 mL of bottled water on another, then incubated both at 30 °C for 48 hours. What is the dependent variable?
questions.answer: **D.** The dependent variable is what is measured.
options: Amount of water on each plate
Number of bacterial colonies on each plate after 48 hours

questions.question: Herd immunity describes a population where the vast majority of people are immunised. Why is herd immunity an effective way to control the spread of infection?
questions.answer:
**D.** With few susceptible people able to carry and pass on the pathogen, chains of transmission break.

*Note: the school accepts B or D. B describes the usual outcome, but unimmunised people are less likely to be exposed, not certain to be protected.*
options: Diseases that originated in cows cannot spread.
Even those who are not immunised will be protected from the pathogen.
Everyone has already had the disease.
There are fewer potential carriers in the population.

questions.question: Tinea (athlete's foot) is caused by a fungus. A person with tinea who walks barefoot leaves some fungal cells behind, which others can pick up as they walk on the floor. What type of disease is tinea, as transmitted this way?
questions.answer: **D.** The fungus passes via a contaminated surface, which is indirect contact.
options: An infectious disease transmitted by a vector
An infectious disease transmitted by direct contact
An infectious disease transmitted by indirect contact

questions.question:
*Eremophila duttonii* is a plant used in traditional Aboriginal medicine. A scientist spread *E. coli* broth evenly over agar plates and placed discs soaked in various substances on each quarter. Results were consistent over repeats (bacteria grew in shaded areas, not in clear areas).

What can be concluded about the *E. duttonii* extract?
questions.answer: **C.** The clear zone around the extract is larger than that of antibiotic A but smaller than that of B.
options: It is an ineffective treatment for bacterial infections.
It is an effective treatment for all bacterial infections.
It is more effective at inhibiting the growth of *E. coli* than antibiotic A.
It is more effective at inhibiting the growth of *E. coli* than antibiotic B.

questions.question:
Rickets is a bone disorder. A rare form that cannot be treated with vitamin D supplements is caused by a mutant allele on the X chromosome. The pedigree shows a family with a history of this condition.

State the genotypes of individuals 3 and 9.
questions.answer: Using $X^R$ for the dominant mutant (rickets) allele and $X^r$ for the normal allele: individual 3 is $X^rY$ and individual 9 is $X^RX^r$.

questions.question:
Rickets is a bone disorder. A rare form that cannot be treated with vitamin D supplements is caused by a mutant allele on the X chromosome. The pedigree shows a family with a history of this condition.

Explain why all the daughters of individuals 1 and 2 have the disease.
questions.answer:
The condition is **X-linked dominant**. The father, individual 2, is affected, so his genotype is $X^RY$; the mother, individual 1, is unaffected, so she is $X^rX^r$.

Every daughter receives the father's only X chromosome, which carries $X^R$, and an $X^r$ from the mother, giving $X^RX^r$. Because $X^R$ is dominant, one copy causes the disease, so all daughters are affected. Sons receive the father's Y and an $X^r$ from the mother, so are unaffected.

questions.question:
The chart shows which amino acids are coded for by mRNA codons. Leiden factor V thrombophilia, which increases blood clotting, is caused by a mutated version of the gene for factor V, a clotting factor.

Normal mRNA: UCC CUG GAC AGG **CGA** GGA AUA CAG GUA UUU

Mutated mRNA (point mutation): UCC CUG GAC AGG **CAA** GGA AUA CAG GUA UUU

Identify the change in amino acid resulting from the mutation.
questions.answer: Arginine (CGA) changes to glutamine (CAA).

questions.question:
The chart shows which amino acids are coded for by mRNA codons. Leiden factor V thrombophilia, which increases blood clotting, is caused by a mutated version of the gene for factor V, a clotting factor.

Normal mRNA: UCC CUG GAC AGG **CGA** GGA AUA CAG GUA UUU

Mutated mRNA (point mutation): UCC CUG GAC AGG **CAA** GGA AUA CAG GUA UUU

The DNA sequence AAA ATA CGT produces a polypeptide with the amino acid sequence Phe–Tyr–Ala. Draw a flow chart showing ONE other type of point mutation (different from the type causing thrombophilia above) in this DNA sequence, and its effect on the polypeptide.
questions.answer:
A **base insertion** (frameshift), inserting T after the fifth base:

Original DNA: AAA ATA CGT → mRNA: UUU UAU GCA → Phe – Tyr – Ala

↓ insertion of T

Mutated DNA: AAA AT**T** ACG T

↓ transcription

mRNA: UUU UA**A** UGC A

↓ translation

Polypeptide: Phe – **Stop**

The new stop codon ends translation early, giving a truncated and probably non-functional polypeptide. (A deletion is equally acceptable.)

questions.question: Describe the effects of a named genetic disease caused by a chromosomal mutation.
questions.answer: **Down syndrome** (trisomy 21) results from an extra copy of chromosome 21, usually through non-disjunction in meiosis. Its effects include intellectual disability, characteristic facial features, short stature, low muscle tone and a higher risk of heart defects.

questions.question:
The human menstrual cycle is controlled by four hormones. FSH and LH are made by the pituitary gland; oestrogen and progesterone are made in the ovaries.

1. **FSH** stimulates the "ripening" of an egg. As the follicle develops it produces **oestrogen** which, among other things, "switches off" **FSH** production so that only one egg ripens at once.
2. **LH** levels remain low throughout the cycle, except for a sudden surge which triggers ovulation on about day 14.
3. The follicle which released the egg then produces **progesterone**, which makes the uterus lining receptive to a fertilised egg.
4. After about 22 days, if fertilisation has not occurred, **progesterone** and **oestrogen** levels drop. Once below a certain level, menstruation is triggered around day 28.

Draw labelled axes (hormone concentration against day, 0–28) and use the information to represent graphically the changing levels of all four hormones.
questions.answer:
Key features:

- **FSH:** raised early in the cycle, falls as oestrogen rises, with a small peak at ovulation.
- **LH:** low except for a sharp surge at about day 14.
- **Oestrogen:** rises as the follicle develops, peaks just before ovulation, has a second smaller rise, then falls after about day 22.
- **Progesterone:** low until ovulation, rises to a peak around day 21, then falls towards day 28.

questions.question:
The human menstrual cycle is controlled by four hormones. FSH and LH are made by the pituitary gland; oestrogen and progesterone are made in the ovaries.

1. **FSH** stimulates the "ripening" of an egg. As the follicle develops it produces **oestrogen** which, among other things, "switches off" **FSH** production so that only one egg ripens at once.
2. **LH** levels remain low throughout the cycle, except for a sudden surge which triggers ovulation on about day 14.
3. The follicle which released the egg then produces **progesterone**, which makes the uterus lining receptive to a fertilised egg.
4. After about 22 days, if fertilisation has not occurred, **progesterone** and **oestrogen** levels drop. Once below a certain level, menstruation is triggered around day 28.

Describe a negative feedback relationship between two of the hormones.
questions.answer: **FSH and oestrogen.** FSH from the pituitary stimulates a follicle to develop. The growing follicle secretes oestrogen. Rising oestrogen acts back on the pituitary (and hypothalamus) to reduce FSH release. With less FSH, further follicles are not stimulated. The product of the process therefore inhibits the signal that caused it, which is negative feedback.

questions.question:
The human menstrual cycle is controlled by four hormones. FSH and LH are made by the pituitary gland; oestrogen and progesterone are made in the ovaries.

1. **FSH** stimulates the "ripening" of an egg. As the follicle develops it produces **oestrogen** which, among other things, "switches off" **FSH** production so that only one egg ripens at once.
2. **LH** levels remain low throughout the cycle, except for a sudden surge which triggers ovulation on about day 14.
3. The follicle which released the egg then produces **progesterone**, which makes the uterus lining receptive to a fertilised egg.
4. After about 22 days, if fertilisation has not occurred, **progesterone** and **oestrogen** levels drop. Once below a certain level, menstruation is triggered around day 28.

Why is this negative feedback (between two of the hormones, such as FSH and oestrogen) needed?
questions.answer:
For FSH and oestrogen, it ensures that only one egg ripens at a time (and keeps hormone levels controlled).

*Note: the school's answer, "to end the menstrual cycle", applies to its example of progesterone suppressing LH, which leads to menstruation.*

questions.question:
Homeostasis can be said to consist of two stages:

- detecting changes from the stable state;
- counteracting changes from the stable state.

Justify this statement with reference to a named example.
questions.answer:
Homeostasis keeps the internal environment close to a set point, for example a human core body temperature of about 37 °C, at which enzymes work efficiently. It operates through negative feedback.

**Stage 1: detection.** Thermoreceptors in the skin and in the hypothalamus detect changes in skin and blood temperature. The hypothalamus compares the information with the set point.

**Stage 2: counteraction.** The hypothalamus signals effectors to oppose the change.

- If temperature rises: sweat glands secrete sweat, which cools the skin as it evaporates, and skin arterioles dilate so more heat is lost.
- If temperature falls: skin arterioles constrict to conserve heat, skeletal muscles shiver to generate heat, and metabolic rate may increase.

As the temperature returns to the set point, the receptors detect this and the responses are switched off.

The statement is justified: without detection the body could not know a response was needed, and without counteraction detecting a change would not restore stability. Both stages are essential parts of the negative feedback loop.

questions.question:
Researchers have studied mRNA vaccines for decades. The first mRNA vaccine to be used widely is one for COVID-19. The diagram outlines the mechanisms involved in the production and activity of the vaccine.

Use the information in the diagram to describe how this vaccine produces the molecule that stimulates the immune response.
questions.answer: The vaccine contains mRNA coding for the virus's spike protein, enclosed in a lipid nanoparticle. After injection the particle is taken up by a host cell and releases the mRNA into the cytoplasm (it does not enter the nucleus). Ribosomes translate the mRNA, producing many copies of the spike protein. The spike protein, which is the antigen, leaves the cell, where antigen-presenting cells detect it.

questions.question:
Researchers have studied mRNA vaccines for decades. The first mRNA vaccine to be used widely is one for COVID-19. The diagram outlines the mechanisms involved in the production and activity of the vaccine.

Explain how immunity against COVID-19 develops as a result of receiving the vaccine.
questions.answer:
Antigen-presenting cells such as macrophages and dendritic cells engulf the spike protein and display fragments of it on their surface to helper T cells. Activated helper T cells stimulate:

- B cells with matching receptors to divide into plasma cells, which secrete antibodies specific to the spike protein (humoral response);
- cytotoxic T cells, which destroy body cells displaying the antigen (cell-mediated response).

Memory B and memory T cells remain. If the virus later enters the body, they respond faster and more strongly, usually preventing serious disease. This is active, artificially acquired immunity.

questions.question:
The cross-section of a porcupine grass leaf looks different when environmental conditions change. The diagrams show the leaf open and the leaf rolled.

Explain which form occurs under dry conditions, referring to one adaptation shown.
questions.answer: The **rolled** leaf occurs in dry conditions. Rolling encloses many of the stomatal grooves, trapping moist air next to the stomata. This reduces the water vapour concentration gradient and so reduces water loss by transpiration. It also reduces the exposed surface area.

questions.question:
The table shows the number of stomates on the leaves of several plant species.

| Plant species | Upper epidermis (per cm$^2$) | Lower epidermis (per cm$^2$) |
|---|---|---|
| A | 4000 | 28 100 |
| B | 1300 | 0 |
| C | 70 | 290 |

Identify the plant most likely to live in an arid environment and use the information to outline how it reduces water loss.
questions.answer:
**Plant C.** It has only 360 stomates per cm$^2$ in total, about 89 times fewer than plant A, so there are far fewer openings for water vapour to diffuse through during transpiration. About 80% of them are on the lower surface, which is shaded and cooler, further reducing evaporation.

(B's stomates are all on the upper surface, which is typical of floating aquatic leaves.)

questions.answer: Set up several replicate tubes for each condition (and repeat the whole experiment), then compare the counts and average them after excluding outliers. Consistent results between repeats show the results are reliable.

questions.question:
The graph shows mortality from lung cancer by gender in Queensland, 1982 to 2002.

Suggest a reason for using a large population sample when comparing rates of lung cancer.
questions.answer: A large sample reduces the effect of chance variation and individual differences, so the rates are more reliable and representative of the population.

questions.question:
The graph shows mortality from lung cancer by gender in Queensland, 1982 to 2002.

Identify TWO trends apparent in the graph.
questions.answer:
1. Male lung cancer mortality **decreased**, from about 73 per 100 000 in 1982 to about 55 per 100 000 in 2002.
2. Female mortality **increased**, from about 12 per 100 000 in 1982 to about 25 per 100 000 in 2002.

(Male mortality also remained higher than female mortality throughout.)

*Note: the school reads the 2002 female value as about 22; the plotted point is nearer 25.*

questions.question:
The graph shows mortality from lung cancer by gender in Queensland, 1982 to 2002.

Outline a possible reason for EACH of the two trends (male and female mortality).
questions.answer:
- **Males:** fewer men smoked in the decades before and during the period, following health campaigns about smoking, so fewer died of lung cancer (earlier detection and better treatment may also contribute).
- **Females:** smoking became more common among women later than among men. Because lung cancer takes decades to develop, deaths from that increased uptake appeared during this period.

questions.question: Artificial insemination is one of the processes used in agriculture to control characteristics in populations of farmed animals. Using specific examples, assess the use of biotechnologies in agriculture and their potential impact on biodiversity.
questions.answer:
Agricultural biotechnology uses organisms and biological processes to improve production. It brings large benefits but tends to reduce genetic diversity unless managed.

**Artificial insemination (AI).** Semen is collected from males with desirable traits, such as dairy bulls whose daughters give high milk yields, then frozen, transported and used to inseminate many females. It spreads desirable alleles quickly and cheaply, without moving animals. However, one bull can father many thousands of calves. The offspring are half-siblings, so allele variety in the herd or breed falls, inbreeding rises, harmful recessive alleles are more likely to be expressed, and the population is more vulnerable to a new disease.

**Transgenic Bt cotton.** A gene from the bacterium *Bacillus thuringiensis* is inserted into cotton, which then makes a protein toxic to caterpillar pests. It has greatly reduced insecticide spraying in Australia, which protects many non-target insects and so can increase biodiversity around crops, and lowers costs and health risks. On the other hand, growing a few modified varieties over large areas narrows crop genetic diversity, caterpillar numbers (food for other species) fall, and pests exposed continuously to the toxin are selected for resistance, so refuge crops are required.

**Assessment.** Both technologies are highly effective for productivity. Their effect on biodiversity depends on management: AI and a few elite crop varieties reduce genetic diversity within farmed species, while reduced pesticide use can benefit wild species. Their use is worthwhile provided many sires and varieties are kept, genetic material of other breeds and varieties is conserved in gene banks, and resistance is monitored.

questions.question:
Alpha-1-antitrypsin (AAT) deficiency is a genetic disease that causes serious lung or liver disease in humans. Sheep can be genetically engineered to produce the human protein AAT in their milk, as shown.

Identify the type of organism produced using this technology.
questions.answer: A **transgenic** organism (it carries a gene from another species).

questions.question:
Alpha-1-antitrypsin (AAT) deficiency is a genetic disease that causes serious lung or liver disease in humans. Sheep can be genetically engineered to produce the human protein AAT in their milk, as shown.

Using this example, discuss ethical and social considerations of producing products using this technology.
questions.answer:
**Social considerations.** For: AAT from sheep milk could treat people with the deficiency, improving their health and ability to work and reducing health care costs; milk can yield large amounts of the protein. Against: development is expensive, so the treatment may not be affordable to all; patients may be wary of possible allergic reactions or unknown risks from an animal-derived product.

**Ethical considerations.** For: relieving serious human suffering is a strong moral reason to use the technology. Against: the sheep are used as production tools; microinjection has a high failure rate, with embryo losses and possible health problems for the animals, and some people object to moving genes between species.

Overall, the benefit to patients can justify the technology if animal welfare is protected, the product is thoroughly tested and access is fair.

questions.question:
An allele has a frequency of 50% in a large breeding population of a mammal on a mainland. Twenty individuals from this population suddenly become isolated on an island. The graph shows the predicted allele frequency in both populations over 140 generations.

Define the term *allele frequency*.
questions.answer: Allele frequency is the proportion of all copies of a gene in a population that are a particular allele.

questions.question:
An allele has a frequency of 50% in a large breeding population of a mammal on a mainland. Twenty individuals from this population suddenly become isolated on an island. The graph shows the predicted allele frequency in both populations over 140 generations.

Justify the difference between the two populations shown on the graph.
questions.answer:
The difference is due to **genetic drift**: random changes in allele frequency from chance differences in which individuals survive and reproduce.

In the large mainland population chance events average out, so the frequency stays close to 50%. The island population began with only 20 individuals (a founder effect), so each chance event changes the proportion substantially. Its frequency fluctuates widely and by generation 140 reaches 0%: the allele has been lost, which is far more likely in a small population.

questions.question:
Sickle cell anaemia is caused by a single point mutation in a gene for haemoglobin (codon GAG becomes GUG). It is an example of a single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP).

| Country | Malaria prevalence (per 1000) | Sickle cell allele frequency (%) |
|---|---|---|
| Algeria | 2 | 0.8 |
| Democratic Republic of the Congo | 45 | 14.5 |
| Egypt | 1 | 1.5 |
| Ethiopia | 10 | 2.6 |
| Kenya | 25 | 5.3 |
| Sierra Leone | 50 | 16.4 |

Using the data and your understanding of evolution, describe a possible reason for the differences in frequency of the sickle cell allele between countries.
questions.answer: Malaria is a selection pressure. People heterozygous for the sickle cell allele are largely protected against severe malaria without having sickle cell anaemia, so where malaria is common (Sierra Leone, 50 per 1000) they survive and reproduce more often, keeping the allele frequency high (16.4%). Where malaria is rare (Algeria, 2 per 1000) there is no such advantage and the allele stays rare (0.8%).

questions.question:
Ebola is a highly contagious virus that can cause rapid death. It is transmitted between humans by contact and exchange of bodily fluids. The map shows the spread of the Ebola epidemic in West Africa in 2014.

Identify a procedure that countries surrounding Guinea could use to prevent the spread of Ebola.
questions.answer: Quarantine: screen people crossing the border and isolate anyone with symptoms or known exposure (along with contact tracing).

questions.question:
Ebola is a highly contagious virus that can cause rapid death. It is transmitted between humans by contact and exchange of bodily fluids. The map shows the spread of the Ebola epidemic in West Africa in 2014.

Compare the effectiveness of quarantine programs in Senegal and Guinea during this epidemic, using the map.
questions.answer:
Both countries border one another, yet Guinea (red) had a widespread outbreak while Senegal (green) had only isolated cases. This suggests Senegal's quarantine measures were much more effective at stopping imported cases from spreading than those in Guinea.

The comparison has limits: the outbreak began in Guinea, where it spread before it was recognised, and the map does not show what measures either country actually used.

questions.question:
As part of the Biology course, students design and conduct a practical investigation into the microbial testing of water and food samples.

State a hypothesis that could be tested.
questions.answer: Example: if untreated (tank or creek) water and tap water are spread on agar and incubated, the untreated water will produce more microbial colonies than the tap water.

questions.question:
As part of the Biology course, students design and conduct a practical investigation into the microbial testing of water and food samples.

Describe safe work practices for this investigation.
questions.answer:
- Seal the plates with tape after inoculation and never reopen them, since harmful microbes may have grown; dispose of them by autoclaving or bleach.
- Incubate below human body temperature (about 25–30 °C) to avoid favouring human pathogens.
- Wash hands, disinfect benches and cover cuts.

*Note: the school suggests incubating at 40 °C to reduce human pathogens. That is wrong: temperatures near body temperature favour them, so school cultures are incubated at 30 °C or below.*

questions.question:
As part of the Biology course, students design and conduct a practical investigation into the microbial testing of water and food samples.

questions.answer:
Count every colony, large and small, marking each as it is counted, three times per plate, then average. The school's counts (yours will differ somewhat):

| A | 308 | 292 | 320 | 307 |
| B | 67 | 76 | 66 | 70 |

questions.question:
The graphs show information about the effectiveness of antibiotics as a treatment strategy for infectious diseases.

Using the graphs and your own knowledge, evaluate the effectiveness of antibiotics as a treatment strategy for infectious disease.
questions.answer:
Antibiotics are drugs that kill bacteria or stop them reproducing, by targeting structures or processes such as the cell wall, ribosomes or DNA replication that differ from those of human cells.

**Evidence of effectiveness.** The first graph shows the US death rate from infection falling from about 280 per 100 000 in the late 1930s, when sulfa drugs and then penicillin were introduced, to about 60 by the early 1950s: a fall of about 220 per 100 000 in 15 years. All later medical technologies reduced it by only about 20 more over 45 years. Antibiotics also make surgery, chemotherapy and organ transplants much safer. (Better sanitation, nutrition and vaccination also contributed to falling deaths.)

**Limitations.**

- They act only on bacteria, not viruses, fungi in general or prions.
- Resistance: the second graph shows MRSA resistance rising from a few per cent in 1981 to about 60% in the early 2000s, and VRE and FQRP resistance rising to roughly 25–30% over a shorter period. Overuse, incorrect use, unfinished courses and use in livestock select for resistant bacteria, which also share resistance genes. The slight rise in infection deaths after about 1980 on the first graph is consistent with this and with new diseases.
- Side effects, allergies and disruption of normal gut bacteria occur.
- Few new classes of antibiotic are being developed.

**Judgement.** Antibiotics have been extraordinarily effective against bacterial disease, but their effectiveness is declining. They remain essential if used carefully: prescribed only when needed, matched to the pathogen, taken as directed, restricted in agriculture and supported by infection control, vaccination and research into new treatments.
